blocks.en: Abstract
blocks.zh: 摘要

blocks.en: Pixel-space diffusion learns visual representations and image generation jointly in a single end-to-end training stage, without a separately pretrained visual encoder. However, plain pixel-space Transformers still trail leading two-stage latent diffusion models in generation quality and training efficiency. We hypothesize that part of this gap arises from retaining one token per patch throughout the backbone, which does not explicitly encourage a visual hierarchy that summarizes related content at progressively coarser levels. To address this, we introduce Hierarchical Diffusion Transformers (HiT), which progressively group related tokens and represent each group with a single token. The main Transformer bottleneck processes these compact group tokens, and ungrouping restores features to their original image positions. A compression budget regulates the average compression ratio across the batch, allowing group memberships and counts to vary across images and diffusion timesteps during both training and generation. The model exhibits emergent semantic structure, learning to group coherent objects and object parts without segmentation labels. In text-to-image generation, HiT further learns to group caption words with image patches depicting the same concepts, without region annotations. HiT achieves 1.48 FID on ImageNet $256\times256$ and reaches comparable generation quality to JiT using approximately 40\% of its cumulative training FLOPs. For text-to-image generation, HiT exceeds UniLiP's average score across five benchmarks with roughly $6\times$ fewer denoiser parameters and $3\times$ fewer forward FLOPs. These results suggest that learning a visual hierarchy within the generator breaks down the barrier to stronger image generation without external visual pretraining.

blocks.en: 1  Introduction
blocks.zh: 导言

blocks.en:
Latent diffusion models exploit a hierarchy between pixels and
compact visual representations [ 31 , 30 , 47 , 44 ] .
A separately trained encoder organizes image information into
a feature space, where a diffusion model subsequently learns
its distribution. This hierarchy reduces the burden of direct
pixel modeling and supplies an organizational prior.
Despite their benefits for generation quality and convergence,
latent diffusion models inherit visual organization shaped
by encoder architectures and pretraining objectives outside
generative training.
Their hierarchical modeling therefore depends on a separate
visual representation learning stage.

blocks.en:
Pixel-space diffusion removes this separate stage by learning
to generate images directly through end-to-end
training [ 17 , 18 , 8 , 45 , 24 ] .
This simplifies the training pipeline, yet matching leading
latent-space models in generation quality and convergence
speed remains challenging.
We hypothesize that part of this gap concerns how visual
information is organized.
During encoder pretraining, latent-space models learn a
visual hierarchy that progressively aggregates fine-grained
image information into compact, higher-level representations.
Pixel-space generators must instead develop such organization
within generative training itself.
This raises the central question of this paper: Can a pixel-space model learn a useful visual hierarchy
within generative training, while retaining an end-to-end
visual pipeline?

By contrast, a regular patch grid fixes this allocation
spatially, assigning the same number of tokens to equally

relevant content [ 12 ] .
This suggests learning the allocation itself rather than
prescribing it through a fixed spatial partition.
This motivates a learnable computational bottleneck that
jointly determines how image information is organized
and how many units are used to represent it.

blocks.en:
To this end, we introduce Hierarchical Diffusion Transformers
(HiT), a new architecture that learns a visual hierarchy
within a single end-to-end pixel-space generator inspired by
H-Net [ 20 , 4 ] .
Our central idea is to group image patch features at successive
stages and process the resulting group tokens in deeper
Transformer bottlenecks.
To realize this design, we use a learned router to group
these features and soft aggregation to form compact tokens,
so deeper Transformer stages operate on progressively
shorter sequences.
We then use ungrouping to return processed group features
to finer positions and refine them with the remaining
Transformer blocks.
We use an aggregate compression budget to regulate the average
token reduction across a batch, allowing the model to allocate
different numbers of groups according to each image’s content
and diffusion timestep.

blocks.en: 2  Related Work
blocks.zh: 2 相关工作

blocks.en:
Latent diffusion learns with compact representations supplied by pretrained autoencoders [ 31 , 30 ] . Subsequent work further incorporates pretrained semantic encoders either as supervision for intermediate denoiser representations or as the generation space itself [ 44 , 47 ] . These approaches benefit from visual organization learned outside the generative objective. Pixel-space methods instead pursue direct generation in one stage [ 17 , 18 , 8 , 45 ] . JiT improves pixel-space generation through clean-image
prediction, while MiniT2I combines this formulation with
joint image–text attention for text-conditioned
generation [ 24 , 38 ] . In these models, the architecture fixes the number and
spatial layout of image tokens at each stage.

blocks.en: 5  Conclusion
blocks.zh: 5 结论

blocks.en:
We introduced HiT, which learns a visual hierarchy within
a single end-to-end pixel-space generator.
By grouping related features into compact units, HiT
organizes visual information while reducing the cost
of deeper processing.
The learned groups capture coherent object structure and
image–text associations without region annotations.
HiT achieves 1.48 FID on ImageNet, reaches JiT’s quality
with substantially less training compute, and outperforms
MiniT2I across five text-to-image benchmarks.
These results support learned visual hierarchy as a
foundation for strong, efficient pixel-space generation
without separate visual pretraining.
